title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps
web_title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps
book_title: Chapter 7: Why the Stock Trades Here — Market Expectations vs. Peers
question: What is the market paying for at ₹1,458.40, how does that compare with what this stock and its peers have been paid before, and how much of the good news is already in the price?

epigraph.quote: Price is what you pay. Value is what you get.
epigraph.author: Warren Buffett, Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letter, 2008 (crediting Ben Graham)

web_blocks.text: Start with what ₹1,458.40 buys. On the 13 November 2026 close the company is worth ₹2,190 Cr across 1,50,16,675 shares [47][43]. Its enterprise value is ₹2,188 Cr. Cash and bank balances of ₹224 Cr at 30 September 2026 exceed borrowings of ₹194 Cr by ₹30 Cr, and the ₹28 Cr book value of minority holders in the Hong Kong subsidiary is added back [46]. Those two numbers matter less than the one that links price to profit. A distributor's price is a bet on how many years of today's earnings the market will pay for in advance. Here the answer is 30.7 years of trailing profit. How the stock got there is more instructive than the number.

web_blocks.caption: Valuation ledger at the 13 November 2026 close of ₹1,458.40 (consolidated; TTM = trailing twelve months to 30 September 2026)
rows: ₹1,458.40 ÷ ₹47.44: FY26 EPS ₹41.04 − H1 FY26 ₹16.77 + H1 FY27 ₹23.17, profit of the parent's owners only [46][47]
The anchor for this report, because it counts only profit that belongs to CNL shareholders
Price ÷ ₹53.70, the sum of the last four quarterly EPS prints (₹15.56 + ₹11.85 + ₹9.02 + ₹17.27), taken before the 12% of profit that belongs to minority holders [44]
Flatters by 3.5 turns; it divides by 13% more earnings than the owners receive
Lands between the two, so 30.7x is not an outlier
What a buyer pays for the last full financial year
A mechanical figure, not a forecast; the explicit forecast follows below
Book value ₹267 per share: attributable equity ₹400.97 Cr ÷ 1.50167 Cr shares [46]
5.5 times book for a business that earned a return on equity of about 20% [43]
EV ₹2,188 Cr ÷ TTM EBITDA ₹127.23 Cr (company basis, including other income): FY26 ₹103.95 Cr − H1 FY26 ₹41.73 Cr + H1 FY27 ₹65.01 Cr [46]
Rich for a distributor, middling for a brand owner
The profit return on price before any growth and before the question of cash conversion
EV ÷ TTM total income of ₹2,892 Cr [46]
Useful only as a yardstick for the Zicom SaaS price below; sales multiples mean little at a 3% to 5% margin
web_blocks.takeaway: Every sensible basis puts the multiple between 27x and 36x; the lowest figure, Screener's 27.2x, divides price by profit that partly belongs to someone else. [44][46][47]

web_blocks.text: The reconciliation matters because the lower multiple is the one a casual reader meets first. Screener sums four quarterly EPS prints on total profit. Yet 12% of consolidated profit after tax in FY26 went to minority holders of Secure Connection, the Hong Kong licensing subsidiary [47]. Our TTM figure rebuilds EPS from the audited FY26 number and the two reviewed half-years, all on the owners' share. It is the figure a shareholder actually owns [46][47]. Two further adjustments push the multiple one way. The ₹30 Cr of net cash comes from ₹683 Cr of non-interest-bearing funding at 30 September. That funding is ₹467 Cr of trade payables and ₹216 Cr of other current liabilities [46]. In Chapter 6 we estimated that 60% to 70% of the ₹479 Cr rise in payables and advances unwinds over three to four quarters. That would turn ₹30 Cr of net cash into net debt of ₹260 Cr to ₹310 Cr. On that footing enterprise value is ₹2,478 Cr to ₹2,528 Cr and EV/EBITDA is 19.5x to 19.9x, not 17.2x.

web_blocks.the_number: A new buyer at ₹1,458.40 needs EPS of about ₹82 to ₹103 three years from now to earn 12% a year. Five years out the need is ₹103 to ₹129, against ₹47.44 today. That is 17% to 29% annual EPS growth, depending on the multiple the stock carries at the end.
web_blocks.how_calculated: Required future price = ₹1,458.40 × 1.12 to the power of the number of years: ₹2,049 after three years and ₹2,570 after five. Required EPS = that price ÷ the exit multiple, at 25x (₹82 over three years, ₹103 over five) and 20x (₹102 over three years, ₹129 over five). Annual growth is the rate that takes ₹47.44 to that EPS.
web_blocks.the_inputs: CMP ₹1,458.40 (13 Nov 2026 close) [43]; attributable TTM EPS ₹47.44 [46][47]; hurdle 12% a year; exit multiples 20x and 25x. Our scenario work and the profit-mix cross-check below support that range. No dividend (yield 0.03%) [44].
web_blocks.the_range: At a 15x exit the five-year EPS need rises to ₹171 (29% a year); at 30x it falls to ₹86 (12.5% a year). A 15% hurdle at a 25x exit needs ₹117 (19.9% a year). Over the last seven years the company delivered 35.0% a year. On that history the lower half of the range is within reach and the upper half is not.
web_blocks.if_off: If the exit multiple is 5 turns lower, the EPS requirement rises about 25% and the growth needed climbs by roughly 5 percentage points a year. If the company converts profit to cash at only half its reported rate, the exit multiple is more likely to fall than to hold. That is the more probable way for this estimate to be wrong. [44][46]

web_blocks.title: Where the last twelve months of gain came from

web_blocks.caption: Price gain split into earnings growth and multiple change (consolidated, per-share, attributable unless stated)
headers: Share of the log gain from EPS vs. multiple
rows: 30 Mar 2026 (last March session) to 13 Nov 2026, 7.5 months
web_blocks.takeaway: On either window the larger part of the gain is the market paying more for each rupee of profit, not the company earning more rupees. A re-rating of that size is the part of a stock's return that can reverse fastest. [43][44][46]

web_blocks.text: Read the first row slowly. In seven and a half months, earnings per share rose 15.6% and the multiple rose 2.4 times. The company reported three sets of results in that time: Q4 FY26, Q1 FY27 and Q2 FY27. The operating margin moved from 3.4% in FY26 to about 5% in H1 FY27 [44][46]. A fair reading is that the market has taken a margin improvement it can see, a brand-mix story it can believe and a stack of announcements it cannot yet measure. It has capitalised all three at once. That is not irrational. It does mean the price now carries expectations that the earnings line has not yet delivered. A buyer who holds from here earns the return on those expectations, not on the past gain.

web_blocks.title: What moved the stock since July, and what the 31 October fund-raise notice authorised

web_blocks.caption: The five biggest price events of the 2026 surge (NSE daily closes; volume per exchange bars, 30-day average about 40,000 shares)
rows: Board approves a budget of up to US$4 million to buy Infinova (India), a Pune surveillance maker, with brand rights for India [54]
No company filing found; nine trading firms appear on both the buy and sell side of the bulk-deal tape [54]
56.5 lakh shares on exchange bars; one intraday report put turnover at ₹149 Cr [43][54]
Q2 FY27 results of 28 October and the call: revenue +14.8%, consolidated profit +36.9% [48][54]
Board approves the Zicom SaaS acquisition and a Singapore procurement subsidiary [50]
AT&T brand licence for networking and data-centre products announced [51]
+0.6% to ₹1,475.00, after an intraday high of ₹1,550.20
web_blocks.takeaway: Only one of the five moves, the results, came with reported numbers. The others followed announcements of intent or trading-desk activity, so the price is paying for optionality that the next two quarters have to convert into revenue. [43][48][50][51][54]

web_blocks.text: The 31 October board notice is the item most likely to be misread. It said the board would meet on 4 November 2026 to “consider and evaluate various fund-raising options, including the issuance of securities other than cash, for financing the proposed acquisitions by the Company” [49]. The outcome is on file, and it is small. The board did not authorise a qualified institutional placement, a warrant issue or any cash equity. It approved buying 100% of Zicom SaaS Private Limited for an enterprise value of about ₹50.50 Cr. Zicom SaaS had FY26 revenue of ₹20.09 Cr, net worth of ₹25.62 Cr and total assets of ₹52.55 Cr. The price is ₹25.00 Cr in cash and ₹25.50 Cr by a preferential issue of up to 2,25,000 shares of face value ₹10 to Onyx SaaS Private Limited. The indicative issue price is ₹1,133.33 a share, subject to the SEBI pricing formula and to shareholders at an extraordinary meeting on 28 November 2026 [50]. The allottee would hold 1.48% after the issue [50]. It also approved a Singapore procurement subsidiary [50]. Completion is expected within three months [50].

Three observations follow. First, the dilution is 1.5% of the share count, and at the 13 November close the shares to be issued are worth ₹32.8 Cr against ₹25.50 Cr of consideration. The indicative price sits 22% below the market because the SEBI formula averages past trading prices. A higher price when the EGM fixes it would mean fewer shares. Second, ₹50.50 Cr for ₹20.09 Cr of revenue is 2.5 times sales, while the whole company trades at 0.76 times. The acquirer is paying a managed-services multiple for recurring-revenue potential [46][50]. Third, management had set the expectation on the 29 October call. Ketan Patel was asked about equity raising. He said that if an opportunity arose “to acquire a brand” or do “something like Infinova but on a larger scale then we will have to then raise capital for sure. But we are waiting for the right time. Currently, banks have been supportive and cash flows are good” [48]. Nothing in the 4 November outcome contradicts that. A larger cash raise remains a live possibility, not an authorised one.

The AT&T agreement, filed on 12 November, adds a licence to make and sell AT&T-branded containment, copper, data-centre networking, fibre, outside-plant and structured-cabling products. India comes first, with Southeast Asia, the Middle East, Africa, New Zealand and Australia to follow in phases and subject to approvals [51]. The filing discloses no royalty, term, minimum guarantee, revenue target or capital need [51]. That is why it counts as optionality. The stock was up as much as 5.7% intraday on it and gave most of that back by the close [43][54].

web_blocks.title: Past stock cycles: five falls of 41% to 51% in nine years

web_blocks.caption: Every drawdown over 30% since the July 2017 listing (NSE daily closes, bonus-adjusted; peak and trough are closing prices)
headers: What the filings show over the same window
rows: First year after the April 2017 IPO at ₹75 on NSE Emerge [47]; FY19 sales ₹368 Cr, operating margin 2.8%, operating cash flow −₹4 Cr [44]
The Covid crash; FY21 sales rose 14% to ₹520 Cr but the operating margin dipped to 2.4% [44]
A micro-cap swept down in the second Covid wave; the stock then rose from ₹84 to ₹746 in ten months [43]
Sales +82% in FY22 and +47% in FY23, EPS +47% in FY23, operating cash flow −₹19 Cr and −₹21 Cr [44]; trailing P/E from 56.0x to 18.6x; ₹80.10 Cr preferential issue at ₹450 announced in June 2023 [47]

FY25 sales +4% (Q1 FY25 −36% YoY) [44]; a 25.6% fall in February 2025 alone [43]; then FY26 sales +52% but operating cash flow −₹271.88 Cr, receivables ₹237.77 Cr to ₹565.11 Cr and borrowings ₹72 Cr to ₹324 Cr [47]; trailing P/E from 33.6x to 12.9x
web_blocks.takeaway: The stock has fallen 41% to 51% five times, and each fall was mostly a collapse in the multiple while earnings rose. Every one was recovered within 0.8 to 6.2 months of the trough, which is why the pattern invites complacency. [43][44][47]

web_blocks.text: Three lessons sit in the table. First, the falls were multiple events, not earnings events. In the 2022-23 decline the stock lost 51% while EPS rose 47%, because the trailing P/E fell from 56.0x to 18.6x. In the 2024-26 decline the multiple fell from 33.6x to 12.9x while EPS rose 31% [44][47]. Second, every drawdown was recovered, and quickly. The price regained its prior peak within 5.5, 1.5, 0.8, 6.2 and 4.2 months of the trough. From each trough the best close within the next twelve months was 91%, 199%, 787%, 139% and 179% higher [43]. That is survivorship you should respect for what it is. The company kept growing profit through all five, and the stock was a V-shaped recovery five times out of five. Third, this is the sixth swing, not the first. From the June 2021 low of ₹84.10 the stock rose to ₹746.00 in March 2022 (8.9 times in ten months) before the 51% fall. From the March 2026 low of ₹528.15 it has risen to ₹1,475.00 (2.8 times in seven and a half months) [43].

web_blocks.caption: Trailing P/E at each March close and now (price ÷ EPS of the fiscal year just ended; Screener annual EPS, FY26 per the annual report)
web_blocks.takeaway: The eight March readings run from 10.7x to 54.3x with a median of 17.3x (22.8x across FY22 to FY26). Today's 30.7x sits above seven of the eight, and only the 2022 peak was higher. [43][44][47]

web_blocks.text: Each March reading divides by the year's full EPS, which was not yet public on the day. The true trailing multiple at the time was somewhat higher than shown, so the comparison is mildly generous to the past. Even so, today's 30.7x is neither unprecedented nor ordinary. It is within the band the stock has reached at peaks: 33.6x in December 2024 and 56.0x in March 2022. It is also well above the 12.9x to 24.5x range where the stock has spent most of the last five years. If the multiple reverted to the FY22-FY26 March median of 22.8x on today's TTM EPS, the stock would be at ₹1,082. That is a statement about what a history-based multiple implies, not a forecast.

web_blocks.title: Reverse DCF: what today's price already assumes

web_blocks.caption: Five-year reverse DCF from ₹1,458.40 (TTM EPS ₹47.44; the EPS the company must reach so that a buyer today earns the hurdle after exiting at the stated P/E)
web_blocks.takeaway: Even the friendliest cell (12% hurdle, 30x exit) needs EPS to nearly double. The middle cells need it to triple in five years, a pace only a handful of Indian companies of this size have sustained. [43][46]

web_blocks.text: Set the grid against the record. EPS compounded at 35.0% a year from FY19 (₹5.04) to FY26 (₹41.20) and 32.6% a year from FY22 (₹13.32), per Screener's annual series [44]. The grid's middle cells, 17% to 25% a year, are below that pace, which is the bull argument. The bear answer is that those years ran from a base about one-ninth of today's EPS. Cumulative operating cash flow over FY19 to FY26 was −₹328 Cr against ₹241 Cr of profit, so the compounding was financed by borrowing and by suppliers, not by cash earned. The next five years would need similar growth from earnings nine times FY19's, while paying for it differently [44][47].

Management's own target frames the upside. It aims for ₹6,000 Cr of FY29 revenue, with 40% from the brand business, up from 14% in FY26 and 19% in Q2 FY27. The target PAT margin is 4.5% to 5% [48]. On that margin the profit would be ₹270 Cr to ₹300 Cr. EPS would be about ₹159 to ₹177 on today's share count, above the ₹147 the grid needs at a 15% hurdle and a 20x exit. So if the target lands, today's price is cheap. The difficulty is the odds. Chapter 5 put the probability of reaching ₹6,000 Cr of revenue at about one in four. It put the probability-weighted FY29 revenue at ₹5,280 Cr, and the chance that brands reach 40% of revenue at under one in ten. Management itself says that “you should not be overconfident” [48].

web_blocks.caption: Chapter 5's four FY29 revenue cases converted to EPS and value (our PAT margin assumptions, lower than management's 4.5% to 5% target; owners' share 88.5%; 1.50167 Cr shares; FY29 treated as three years away)
web_blocks.takeaway: On Chapter 5's odds, a buyer today earns about 7% a year if the stock ends at 20x and about 15% a year if it ends at 25x. The exit multiple, not the revenue case, decides whether the price pays a 12% hurdle. [43][46][48]

web_blocks.text: What is the market paying for? The brand mix moved from 14% of FY26 revenue to 17% in H1 FY27 and 19% in Q2 FY27. The brand segment earned 59% of FY26 segment profit on that sliver of revenue [47][48]. The Honeywell licence, which is up for renewal in March 2027. The surveillance build-out, now with Infinova, Matrix, Sparsh and Zicom SaaS, and the AT&T licence behind it. The FY29 target. Then there is the regulatory flag. The stock sits in NSE's long-term additional surveillance framework, Stage II, which is a trading restriction and not a comment on the company [43][52]. What is the market not paying for? Cash conversion. H1 FY27 operating cash flow was +₹351.24 Cr, about 84% of it from a net release of working capital, mainly payables and advances, rather than profit [46]. The CFO told the same call that 45 days of working capital is not something he expects to hold: “we don't feel that, that is going to be sustainable in the long run”. The normal range is 52 to 55 days [48]. No multiple of 30x is paid for a number its own CFO calls temporary.

web_blocks.title: Scenario valuation: bull, base and bear

web_blocks.caption: Explicit 12-month scenarios (consolidated, total-income basis as the company reports EBITDA; ₹ Cr unless stated; owners' share 88.5% of PAT; 1.50167 Cr shares; our model, valuation_model.py)
rows: H2 FY27 income +26% YoY, FY28 +30%; EBITDA margin 5.0% then 5.25%; BharatNet, brand growth and both acquisitions land on time; interest ₹34 Cr in FY28
H2 +15%, FY28 +24%; margin 4.4% then 4.55%; brand mix rises but working capital drifts to 52 to 55 days; interest ₹44 Cr in FY28
H2 +8%, FY28 +8%; margin 3.9% then 3.8%; payables unwind, Honeywell terms reset or renewal slips; interest ₹52 Cr in FY28
web_blocks.takeaway: Only the bull case, a one-in-five outcome, ends above the current price. The weighted value is ₹1,287, 11.7% below ₹1,458.40, and the spread between ₹472 and ₹2,347 is wide enough that the probabilities matter more than any single estimate. [43][46][47][48]

web_blocks.text: These are our assumptions, set against the reported base. H1 FY27 EBITDA was ₹65.01 Cr on ₹1,231.65 Cr of total income, a 5.3% margin. The base case lets the margin settle at 4.4% in the second half because the October-to-March half carried 61% of FY26's revenue, much of it low-margin market-entry volume [44]. It also reflects interest cost, ₹16.92 Cr in H1, which has to rise with working capital [46]. The base FY27E EPS of ₹54.19 is 14% above TTM EPS, which puts the stock on 26.9x FY27E and 22.7x FY28E base earnings. The bull case reaches FY28E EPS of ₹93.90, which would make today's price 15.5 times earnings. The bear case lets EPS fall to ₹33.73 in FY28, 43.2 times at the current price. Management guides FY27 revenue growth of roughly 20% [48], which sits between our base (about 16% on total income) and our bull. H1 growth was 16.6%, so the second half would need to grow about 22% to deliver it.

web_blocks.caption: Profit-mix cross-check: a distributor multiple and a brand-owner multiple weighted by where the profit is made (FY26 audited segment result: Brand 59%, Market Entry 41%)
rows: A 70% discount to Aditya Infotech (CP Plus) at 82.4x, a brand owner with a 14.7% operating margin and 28.6% ROCE; CNL's brand profit is about 97% one licence [45]
web_blocks.takeaway: The profit-mix multiple of 20.1x is where our 21x base exit comes from, rounded up one notch for growth faster than any listed distributor. On today's TTM EPS it is worth ₹953, which is the gap the market is paying for in growth. [45][46]

web_blocks.caption: Sensitivity of the 12-month value to FY28E EPS and the exit multiple (₹ a share; percentage versus ₹1,458.40)
web_blocks.takeaway: The current price is 22.7x base-case FY28E EPS and 15.5x bull-case EPS. A 12% return over twelve months would need about 25.4x on base-case earnings or 17.4x on bull-case earnings. It is fairly priced for the base earnings path only if the market keeps paying more than any listed distributor and less than the brand owner. [43][46][45]

web_blocks.title: Peers: where 30.7x sits among distributors and a brand owner

web_blocks.caption: CNL vs. Redington (global-scale distributor), Rashi Peripherals (listed IT distributor) and Aditya Infotech / CP Plus (surveillance brand owner), TradingView and Screener snapshot of 13 November 2026
web_blocks.takeaway: CNL's return on capital matches the two distributors. Its operating margin of 3.9% sits between the distributors' 1.8% and 3.0% and the brand owner's 14.7%. Its multiple sits between the two groups but much closer to the distributors than to the brand owner. TradingView's market cap of ₹2,214.96 Cr for CNL is struck on the 12 November price and its 29.9x P/E uses its own earnings basis; at the 13 November close and attributable earnings the figures are ₹2,190 Cr and 30.7x. [43][44][45]

web_blocks.text: Redington, the global-scale distributor, is worth ₹27,339 Cr at 13.6x on Screener (14.7x on TradingView), 2.5 times book, ROCE 18.4% and a Stage 3 chart. Its stock fell 10.3% in a month [43][45]. Rashi Peripherals, the listed IT distributor, is worth ₹4,579 Cr at 11.9x (12.0x on TradingView), 2.0 times book, ROCE 17.0% and a falling chart (Stage 4 on the snapshot evaluation, Stage 3 on the daily ledger). Its trailing revenue is up 51% yet its stock is down 22.1% in a month and 15.9% in the last week [43][45]. Aditya Infotech, which sells CP Plus cameras, is worth ₹50,886 Cr at 82.4x and 13.9 times book. Its operating margin is 14.7% and ROCE 28.6% [43][45]. CNL's 30.7x is 2.3 times Redington's multiple, 2.6 times Rashi's and 0.37 times the brand owner's. The honest reading is that a blend, not either extreme, is the right anchor. The brand business supplies 59% of CNL's segment profit, so Redington's multiple understates it. But that brand profit is one licence and a sliver of revenue, so CP Plus's multiple overstates it by a distance.

The limits of comparability are real. Redington is 12 times CNL's market value and earns its 1.8% margin on a global balance sheet. Rashi shows the sharpest warning for CNL. It grows faster (+51% against +36%) at a similar return on capital, and the market has put it on 11.9x and cut it 22% in a month. Growth alone has not earned a distributor a premium in this cohort. CP Plus owns its brands and earns four times CNL's margin, so its 82x is a statement about margin and ownership that CNL cannot match today. CNL migrated to the NSE main board in August 2019 and listed on the BSE in December 2025 [47]. What CNL has that the distributors do not is a fast-growing licence business; what it lacks that CP Plus has is a margin and a product it owns. The multiple will go where the brand share and the cash conversion go.

web_blocks.region_era: United States and Latin America, wireless handset distribution, 2006 to 2011
web_blocks.mechanism: A thin-margin handset distributor with one dominant vendor and one dominant country launched its own brand and told investors the brand would lift gross margins. It was priced on growth and that promise before the brand showed up in gross profit. The multiple then converged back as cash and concentration risks surfaced. [53]
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: 2006: net sales $240.9 million (+65%), net income $2.5 million or $0.16 a diluted share. The 10-K reports the closing price ranged from $16.76 to $0.90 between 1 January 2006 and 20 March 2008. At $16.76 against $0.16 of EPS the multiple was about 105 times. 2007: net sales $244.7 million (+2%) and gross profit down 39% to $11.5 million from $18.8 million. There was a net loss of $1.6 million, covenant waivers on a $26.8 million bank line, and the stock at $3.07 on 29 June 2007. Samsung affiliates were 83% of cost of sales in 2007; Argentina was 54% of sales. In 2009 over 95% of roughly $231 million of net sales was Samsung product to Argentine carriers, and an Argentine import rule ended that distribution business in 2011. [53]
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: The vulnerability is the same shape as CNL's: a single licence behind 97% of brand revenue, a largest customer near 25%, and thin distribution margins funded by debt and suppliers. The difference is that CNL's brand mix already shows in gross margin (11.3% in Q2 FY27 against 7.9% a year earlier [46]). Its profit is also audited and growing. The lesson is that a distributor re-rated for a brand story converges back whenever concentration or cash bites; the re-rating lasts only if reported cash conversion confirms it. [53]

web_blocks.title: What the valuation work means for each horizon

web_blocks.text: Short term (weeks to three months). Valuation gives no edge in either direction. A stock at 30x can reach 40x on the next announcement, and one at 30x can fall to 22x on a single disappointing quarter; the history shows both. What does matter is that the price has run 176% in seven and a half months, with 86% of that from the multiple. It also matters that the last session printed only 14,339 shares, 0.36 times the 30-day average. From the top of the technical support zone (₹1,297.52) to the structural stop reference of ₹913.79, risk is ₹383.73 a share. The base case of ₹1,352 gives ₹54.41 of reward (0.14:1). The probability-weighted ₹1,287 gives a slightly negative ratio (−0.03:1), and the bull case of ₹2,347 gives 2.74:1. From today's price the base case is below the market (−0.20:1). Chapter 8 handles timing; the numbers say the base-case reward is small against the risk at this price, and whether and where to act is Chapter 9's call.

Medium term (six to twenty-four months). The valuation will be decided by evidence the company has not yet produced. The evidence is the 31 December balance sheet and a 31 March 2027 balance sheet with working capital at or below 55 days. It also includes the Honeywell renewal due in March 2027 with its royalty terms, the closing of Infinova and Zicom SaaS, and the first revenue from AT&T. A clean run through those items moves the odds toward the bull case and a 25x multiple. A payables unwind or a licence-term reset moves them toward 14x and ₹472. The 50% base case is where a buyer waits for evidence while paying for the optimistic version.

Long term (three to five years). A new buyer needs 17% to 25% annual EPS growth for five years to earn 12% to 15% at a 20x to 25x exit. The company delivered 33% to 35% from a much smaller base, and management's FY29 target has a one-in-four chance. The long-run return from ₹1,458.40 depends more on the multiple at the end than on the revenue path. On Chapter 5's weighted odds it is about 7% a year at 20x and about 15% at 25x. If cash conversion proves structural, the business deserves a brand-owner multiple and today's price may prove modest. If it does not, a distributor multiple on the same earnings gives ₹617 (13x TTM EPS). The final call on the price, the support levels and any action belongs to Chapter 9 and the verdict. [43][46][48]

book_paragraphs: Let me start where every desk conversation about a stock should start, with what you actually get for your money. At ₹1,458.40 you are paying ₹2,190 Cr for Creative Newtech, and the multiple on the profit that belongs to its shareholders is 30.7 times. Notice that I said belongs to its shareholders. The popular screens print 27.2 times, and the difference is a quiet piece of bookkeeping: they add up four quarters of profit before the 12% that goes to the minority partners in the Hong Kong licensing company. Picture the warehouse in Bhiwandi at quarter-end. The goods on the shelves are yours; the partner's share of the licence income is not. When you and I compare this stock with Redington or Rashi, the honest number is 30.7, and the habit of using the flattering one is how cheap stocks get invented.

Now the balance sheet, because enterprise value is the price of the whole business rather than only of its shares. The company holds ₹224 Cr of cash and owes ₹194 Cr to banks, so it looks net cash by ₹30 Cr. I would like that to be true, and I would like you to ask where the cash came from. At 30 September, suppliers were owed ₹467 Cr and customers had paid ₹216 Cr of advances, ₹683 Cr of other people's money in total. Chapter 6 estimated that 60% to 70% of the recent rise in that funding goes back out within three or four quarters, which would turn the small net cash into net debt of ₹260 Cr to ₹310 Cr. Run the same sum on that footing and the stock is on about 19.7 times operating earnings, not 17.2. A balance sheet is a photograph of one day, and this one was taken on a good day.

Here is the part I want you to feel before you see a single table. Between the last March close and today, earnings per share rose 15.6%, and the price multiple rose 2.4 times. The stock went from 12.9 times profit to 30.7 times in seven and a half months. The company did well, but the main thing that changed was the market's willingness to pay. Ask yourself what the owner of a small distribution business would think of an offer that doubled in a quarter without his sales doubling. He would be flattered, and he would also wonder what the buyer knew. I do not say the buyer is wrong. I say that from here you are no longer buying the past gain, only the expectations it was built on.

What were the expectations built on? Look at the calendar. On 13 July the board approved a budget of up to four million dollars for Infinova, and the stock jumped 10.8%. On 4 November it approved Zicom SaaS and the stock rose 17.0% in a day. On 12 November it announced an AT&T licence, touched ₹1,550.20 and closed at ₹1,475. Only the results week came with numbers. And the notice of 31 October about fund-raising? It turned out to mean a share swap: 2,25,000 shares, about 1.5% of the company, to the sellers of Zicom, plus ₹25 Cr of cash. The chairman had told the 29 October call, “If an opportunity where we get to, say, acquire a brand… we will have to then raise capital for sure. But we are waiting for the right time. Currently, banks have been supportive and cash flows are good.” That is the honest position, and I would take him at his word while watching for the day it changes.

History is the best teacher a stock has, so let us read this one. Since the July 2017 listing the price has fallen between 41% and 51% five times. In March 2022 it peaked at ₹746, and thirteen months later it stood at ₹363.20, down 51%. Now look at what the company did over the same months: sales rose, and EPS rose 47% in the year to March 2023. The profit did not fall; the multiple fell from 56 times to 18.6 times. I have sat in many rooms where a promoter explains a falling price by pointing to growing profit, and he is half right. Profit is the floor under a stock, and the multiple is the lift in the elevator. When the lift drops, the floor looks very far down.

There is a comforting half to the story too, and I would be misleading you if I hid it. Each of those five falls was recovered, and quickly: the old peak was back within 0.8 to 6.2 months of each trough. From each low, the best close in the next twelve months was 91%, 199%, 787%, 139% and 179% higher. The market has always rewarded patience in this stock. But be careful with that record. The stock has fallen 41% to 51% five times and recovered five times, which is also the description of a stock whose holders must be willing to sit through a 40% loss and a year of boredom to collect. Today's 30.7 times is above seven of the eight March readings since 2019, which ran from 10.7 to 54.3 times with a median of 17.3. You are buying near the top of the stock's own usual range.

Let me introduce the tool I trust most for this kind of question, the reverse DCF. Instead of forecasting and hoping, you ask what the price needs the business to do. To earn 12% a year for five years at a 20 times exit, earnings per share must go from ₹47.44 to ₹128.50, a 22% annual climb. At a 25 times exit the figure is ₹102.80 and 17% a year. The company did grow EPS 35% a year from FY19 and 33% from FY22, so the arithmetic is not absurd. But I would ask you what it cost. Over eight years the business earned ₹241 Cr and consumed ₹328 Cr of cash in operations. Growth this fast has so far been financed by banks and suppliers, and the next five years begin from earnings nine times those of FY19.

Management's target is the best case for the stock, and it deserves a fair hearing. The CFO told the October call that the brand share should go from 19% to 40% by FY29, adding that “that is very realistic kind of expectation from 19% to 40%.” On revenue of ₹6,000 Cr and the profit margin management aims for, earnings per share would be somewhere between ₹159 and ₹177, which would make today's price look cheap. I gave that outcome about one chance in four in Chapter 5, and the chance that brands reach 40% of revenue at under one in ten. Weighted across all four of those cases and a margin that is lower than management's, FY29 EPS comes to ₹89.30. At 25 times that is worth ₹2,233, and at 20 times ₹1,786. Those two numbers are the whole argument: 15% a year for the optimist's multiple, and 7% a year for the sceptic's.

Now let me say what the market is not paying for, because it is the most important sentence in this chapter. It is not paying for cash. In the first half of this year operating cash flow was +₹351 Cr, and about 84% of that came from a net release of working capital, mainly payables and advances, rather than profit. The same CFO who gave us the 19% to 40% forecast said of the 45-day working-capital figure, “we don't feel that, that is going to be sustainable in the long run,” and called 52 to 55 days normal. When a company's own finance chief calls his best number temporary, nobody should pay 30 times for it. And yet the stock does. That tells me the price is resting on the brand story and the surveillance story, and the cash story is a footnote that the next two balance sheets will either promote or bury.

So I built three worlds and gave each a probability. In the bull world, with a 20% chance, sales grow 26% in the second half and 30% next year, the margin reaches 5.25% and the market pays 25 times: ₹2,347, up 61%. In the base world, with a 50% chance, growth is 15% and 24%, the margin settles at 4.55% and the stock gets 21 times: ₹1,352, down 7%. In the bear world, with a 30% chance, growth fades to 8%, the margin slips to 3.8% and the multiple falls to 14 times: ₹472, down 68%. Weighted together it is ₹1,287, which is 11.7% below today's price. Only the bull case beats the market. I am not saying the bull case will not happen; I am saying that you are being paid for one outcome in five and paying for all of them.

The cross-check from the other side is simple enough to do on the back of an envelope. Take 59% of the profit as brand profit, worth 25 times, and 41% as distribution profit, worth 13 times like Redington and Rashi. The blend is 20.1 times, which is where my 21 times base multiple comes from, with one notch added for growth. Applied to today's earnings it gives ₹953. Applied to next year's base earnings it gives ₹1,293. The peers show how fickle the market can be with distributors. Rashi grew revenue 51%, trades at 11.9 times and fell 22% in a month. Redington fell 10%. CP Plus, which owns its brands and earns a 14.7% margin, trades at 82 times. CNL sits between the two groups because it is partly each, and that is exactly why its multiple is most exposed to news.

I want to leave you with an old story, because I think the shape of it applies. InfoSonics was a Latin American handset distributor, with one big vendor, Samsung, and one big country, Argentina. In 2006 it launched its own brand, verykool, and told investors that owning the product would lift its margins. Sales rose 65% that year, the stock traded as high as $16.76 in the range its own annual report cites, and the earnings behind it were $0.16 a share. A year later gross profit had fallen 39%, the company posted a loss, and the share price was $3.07 by June and $0.90 at its low. I am not comparing the businesses; CNL's brand margin shows up in its audited numbers. I am comparing the vulnerability. Distribution paid the bills, the brand earned the multiple, and a single concentration risk could take both away.

What does all this mean for the three kinds of person who might be reading? If you think in weeks, valuation will not save you or sink you, and the tape chapter that follows is the right tool. If you think in two years, the evidence that decides this is not yet on file: a December balance sheet, a March 2027 one at or below 55 working-capital days, the Honeywell renewal and its royalty terms. If you think in five years, the return from here depends on the multiple at the end more than on the revenue, about 7% a year at 20 times and 15% at 25 on my weighted odds. I have not told you what to do, and I will not do it here. Chapter 9 carries the verdict, and I want you to arrive there knowing exactly what the price assumes.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: The number I would ask you to remember is 2.4. The share price went up 2.76 times since March; earnings per share went up 1.16 times; the rest, a factor of 2.4, is the market's mood. Moods are real and they can last for years, but they are the part of a stock's price that you cannot audit. This stock has halved five times in nine years and recovered every time, and I respect that record. I also know that the way to be wrong in a business like this is to be right about the profit and wrong about what to pay for it.

book_callouts.title: PRICE = PROFIT × THE MULTIPLE, AND ONLY ONE OF THEM IS ON THE AUDIT REPORT
book_callouts.text: Split every price move into two parts, what the company earned and what the market was willing to pay for each rupee. Earnings are checked by an auditor and can be rebuilt from filings. The multiple is checked by nobody; it is set by growth stories, flows and mood. A holder's return is the product of both, so a holder who owns a business that grows profit 20% a year and sees the multiple halve has lost money. Ask, for any price, which of the two is carrying the weight.
